name: Hassan Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a blast-hole drill at a large mine, setting the rig on the marked line and watching how the rock cuts. At 58 I know the sound of a bit starting to wear, though my vocational certificate is the only paper I have for the job. I enjoy getting a clean pattern ready for the blasting crew and hate losing an hour to a fault nobody wrote down. My wife cleans classrooms for a local school, and our grown children live elsewhere. Her pay and my lower mine wage cover the bills, but her dental treatment left us with less than one month's expenses saved; I use AI daily for bulletins and shift notes, then check the answer with the drill manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the blasting crew small AI gains could make fault notes quicker without moving the drill itself. I would say the bit and rock still decide whether the pattern is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can use better records to avoid a missed fault, which could help my standing at the mine. I still watch our dental debt, because the school and mine wages leave little extra at month's end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling the marked pattern and checking bit wear before each run. I'd use my AI note checker to compare fault entries with the manual after each shift. I'd pay an extra small amount toward the dental bill whenever I earn overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technology is useful in small doses, and I am comfortable with that. The household money is the part that feels fragile, even with two wages coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the tool help you catch recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It flagged that I had written the wrong bit number in a shift note. I checked the manual and fixed the entry before the blasting crew used it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How are the dental payments affecting your choices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We postponed replacing the kitchen table and pay the dentist each month. I cannot call that a crisis, but it means there is almost no spare money if my truck breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew planning software may reorder drilling, while people still position rigs on the ground. I would offer to test new drill screens with operators before management changes every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think fewer planning roles could mean tighter drill targets and eventually fewer hours for the slower crews. My daily AI use gives me a head start, but it does not guarantee a seat on the rig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the drill supervisor to include me in a paid trial of the planning screen. I'd compare AI drill plans with actual rock and bit-wear notes for a month. I'd apply for an equipment records post at the mine if drill hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be interested enough to try it and wary enough to keep my notes. The danger is a manager deciding a tidy plan means fewer people, while the rock remains untidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record during that trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write down how often a planned line needs moving because the rock breaks differently from the map. If the software learns that, fine; I want the operators' corrections visible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a records job protect your income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An equipment records job might help for a few years. I do not mistake an equipment records job for permanent shelter from stronger thinking AI. I would apply if our drill hours fell, because the dental payments are due every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2028 thinking AI could run drill plans, but robots able to handle rigs arrive around 2031. I would ask the company for paid apprenticeships before it removes experienced operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect robot rigs around 2031 to threaten my pay before our dental debt is gone. I could learn a different trade, but few nearby mines means a certificate alone may not bring a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the maintenance foreman about funded hydraulic-repair training this month. I'd enroll in paid hydraulic training if it comes with a workshop opening. I'd apply for a maintenance helper post in the next town while I still earn drill wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The speed frightens me, even though I like learning new tools. I wake up calculating how many dental payments we could make on my wife's school wage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 2029 look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still be drilling if people are needed until robots arrive around 2031. At the same time I would try for a paid workshop place; a planning desk would be exposed as soon as full thinking AI arrived in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home after applying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife the application is a chance, not another wage yet. My wife’s school cleaning pay could cover food, but not the whole mortgage and the dentist.

fieldNote: He distinguishes **2028 planning exposure** from the 2031 robot risk to paid drilling.
A **funded workshop opening** matters more than an abstract certificate because his household cannot bridge an unpaid gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2031 thinking AI gives us time to train before robotic rigs arrive around 2034. I would tell the crew to ask for workshop places while the mine still needs skilled hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, I could build a second trade while continuing to earn on the drill. I worry the workshop itself may change after 2034 robots, so training is a bridge rather than a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a hydraulic repair course if the mine pays fees and keeps my drill wages. I'd work drill shifts in 2032 while logging common faults with the maintenance crew. I'd apply for workshop vacancies as soon as the course qualifies me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warning is long enough to learn something useful without jumping off the wage today. I would still feel anxious until I had a paid place on the other side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What fault would you start with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The feed hose leaks often enough that every operator recognizes the smell before the gauge drops. I would ask the fitter to show me the proper replacement, then write down the hours it saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course has no job attached?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take it only if my pay continued and the skill was recognized outside this one mine. Our savings cannot cover a long gap between a certificate and a vacancy.

S3.quote: Our savings cannot cover a long gap between a certificate and a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2036 thinking AI may take the planning desk while robot rigs remain about three years behind. I would tell younger drillers to learn hands-on repairs before the 2039 robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I may want fewer shifts, but I cannot count on retiring with today's savings. By 71 in 2039, I hope to leave the drill, though the dentist and mortgage still shape that choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid drill shifts while my health and the mine allow. I'd clear the dental balance before raising our monthly savings transfer. I'd ask the workshop foreman about part-time repair shifts before 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade lets me plan a slower finish rather than run at the first rumour. No calendar date will pay the mortgage for us. That makes me uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2037 after thinking AI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 69 I would be drilling if the rigs still need operators and I am fit enough, or doing paid repair shifts if the workshop takes me. The AI might already plan the holes, but robots capable of running the rig arrive around 2039 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes and budgets. I would rather clear the dental account and keep earning than treat their pay as our retirement income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest, because a robot rig around 2031 could remove my wage before I have another trade. Paid hydraulic training with an actual workshop opening would help. I would also want honest figures on when the mine plans to replace rigs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You might ask whether the mine will count years of fault finding as skill when it hires for the workshop. My certificate is old, but the feed hose never asked for a new one.

headlineQuote: My certificate is old, but the feed hose never asked for a new one.
portrait: Hassan is a **58-year-old blast-hole drill operator** at a large mine with a vocational certificate and lower pay.
His wife's school cleaning wage helps, but **dental debt** and a mortgage leave less than one month's expenses saved.
He uses **AI daily** to check notes and bulletins, then verifies them against the drill manual.
He seeks **paid hydraulic training** and a workshop opening while keeping retirement tied to actual household costs.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** because robot rigs around 2031 could remove his main wage before retraining.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid hydraulic training**, a workshop vacancy and honest replacement dates from the mine.
